title: Evolutionary repurposing of a metabolic thiolase complex enables antibiotic biosynthesis

paper_content.abstract: The functional diversification of biosynthetic enzymes underlies the chemical richness of natural products, yet how primary metabolic enzymes evolve to acquire specialized functions in secondary metabolism remains elusive. Here, we report a tripartite enzyme complex from oral Streptococcus species—comprising 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl (HMG)-CoA synthase (HMGS), acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase (ACAT), and a DUF35 protein—that catalyzes an unusual Friedel–Crafts C-acetylation on a pyrrolidine-2,4-dione scaffold, completing the biosynthesis of the antibiotic reutericyclin A. Cryo-electron microscopy of the S. macacae-derived thiolase complex (SmaATase) reveals a conserved architecture resembling the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex involved in the mevalonate pathway, yet with key catalytic residues rewired to reprogram substrate specificity. Biochemical characterization, molecular modeling, and evolutionary analysis confirmed that the ancestral activity of HMG-CoA synthesis has been lost, while the complex has been repurposed to mediate Friedel–Crafts C-acylation of small molecule acceptors. These findings reveal a rare example of thiolase complex neofunctionalization, shedding light on an underexplored trajectory in enzyme evolution and offering a template for engineering C–C bond-forming catalysts in synthetic biology.
paper_content.introduction:
Natural products, also known as secondary or specialized metabolites, confer selective advantage to their producing organisms by mediating ecological interactions such as competition, defense, and communication1. In contrast to the relatively conserved structures of primary metabolites, natural products display remarkable chemical diversity, largely driven by the evolutionary plasticity of their biosynthetic enzymes2. This diversity often arises through the recruitment and functional repurposing of primary metabolic enzymes into specialized metabolic pathways2,3. Beyond the well-known fatty acid synthase–polyketide synthase (FAS–PKS) paradigm4,5, notable examples include the evolution of chalcone isomerase from a noncatalytic fatty acid-binding protein6,7, and the emergence of β-lactam synthetases from asparagine synthase8,9 (Supplementary Fig. 1). While the catalytic repertoire of biosynthetic enzymes continues to expand, the evolutionary trajectories by which primary metabolic enzymes—especially multimeric enzyme complexes—acquire new functions in secondary metabolism remain poorly understood.

The thiolase superfamily comprises highly conserved enzymes present across all domains of life and plays essential roles in central metabolic pathways10,11. For instance, acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase (ACAT) catalyzes the formation of acetoacetyl-CoA, a key intermediate in cholesterol and steroid hormone biosynthesis, while its reverse reaction is critical for fatty acid β-oxidation12,13. In archaea, a tripartite enzyme complex composed of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl (HMG)-CoA synthase (HMGS), ACAT, and a DUF35 protein (Pfam family PF01796, Domain of Unknown Function) enables mevalonate biosynthesis by coupling a thermodynamically unfavorable thiolase reaction with a favorable HMG-CoA condensation, thereby facilitating intermediate channeling (Fig. 1a)14. In previous work, we identified a HMGS homolog mucA, a ACAT homolog mucB, and a DUF35 homolog mucC within the muc biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) in Streptococcus mutans (Fig. 1a), which directs the production of the antimicrobial compound reutericyclin A (RTC-A) and the immunomodulatory molecule mutanocyclin15–17. The muc BGC is widely distributed among Firmicutes, particularly in Streptococcus species16. Based on sequence homology and biosynthetic logic, MucABC was hypothesized to be an acyltransferase (ATase) essential for RTC-A biosynthesis15. Its divergence from the canonical role in mevalonate biosynthesis indicates a previously unrecognized evolutionary trajectory within the thiolase superfamily.

Here, we report functional and structural characterization of the MucABC enzyme complex from oral Streptococcus, exemplified by the S. macaca-derived thiolase complex. We show that this enzyme complex catalyzes a non-canonical Friedel–Crafts C-acetylation on a pyrrolidine-2,4-dione scaffold during RTC-A biosynthesis. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and biochemical analyses reveal that the neofunctionalization of this complex involves the loss of conserved catalytic motifs—such as the E–C–H–N tetrad in HMGS and the HDxF motif in ACAT—along with active-site remodeling for specialized substrate recognition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this acetylation step is indispensable for the antimicrobial activity of RTC-A, providing Streptococcus a competitive advantage in its native niche. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized evolutionary trajectory in which multimeric enzyme complexes from primary metabolism are repurposed for secondary metabolic functions, offering opportunities for engineering modular biocatalysts in synthetic biology.
paper_content.results:
Characterization of Streptococcal ATases as Friedel-Crafts acylases

A BLASTP search using the MucABC sequence from S. mutans as the query showed 31–37% sequence identity with PhlACB from Pseudomonas protegens (known as PpATase), a rare Friedel-Crafts acylase known to mediate the reversible disproportionation of phloroglucinol (PG), monoacetylphloroglucinol (MAPG), and 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol (DAPG; Supplementary Fig. 2a)18,19. Although their overall sequence similarity is low, the individual components of MucABC retain conserved domains found in both PpATase and the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex (Supplementary Fig. 3), suggesting a potential conservation of thiolase-related chemistry. To investigate the catalytic activity of mucABC-encoded proteins, we selected three highly similar mucABC operons (89–100% identity) from host-adapted oral streptococci: S. mutans B30 (human), S. macacae NCTC11558 (monkey), and S. troglodytae TKU31 (chimpanzee; Supplementary Fig. 2a). Given that PpATase is functional only when the entire phlACB operon is co-expressed18–20, we constructed a plasmid expressing the full mucABC operon with a C-terminal His6-tag on MucB to facilitate purification (Supplementary Fig. 2b). Of the three variants, S. macacae mucABC exhibited superior expression in Escherichia coli, yielding the highest protein amounts and purity after affinity chromatography (Supplementary Fig. 2c), and was therefore chosen for biochemical characterization.

To perform in vitro enzymatic assays, we chemically synthesized preRTC-A (Supplementary Fig. 4), the presumed nonribosomal peptide synthetase-polyketide synthetase (NRPS-PKS)-derived biosynthetic precursor of RTC-A16. Four unnatural acetyl donors previously shown to be accepted by PpATase—N-acetylimidazole (N-AcIm), isopropenyl acetate (IPEA), ethyl thioacetate (EtSAc), and phenyl acetate (PA)—were tested with MucABC (Fig. 1b). Ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) analysis confirmed the formation of a product peak with identical retention time for all four acetyl donors (Fig. 1b). High-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) analysis of the enzymatic reaction using PA revealed a 42 Da shift from the substrate ion [M−H]- at m/z 306.2087 (Cald. 306.2075) to the production at m/z 348.2187 (Cald. 348.2180), consistent with an acetylation event (Fig. 1b). Scaled-up enzymatic reactions enabled product isolation and confirmation of its identity as RTC-A by 1H and 13C NMR spectroscopy (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 5), with the acetyl group installed at the C-3 position of the pyrrolidine-2,4-dione core (Fig. 1b). No O-acetylated byproducts were detected in time-course analyses (Supplementary Fig. 6a). Since the chemically synthesized preRTC-A was obtained as a racemic mixture (due to the acidity of the α-proton), we further isolated the individual (R)- and (S)-preRTC-A via chiral separation. UPLC analysis confirmed that MucABC could utilize both enantiomers as substrate, as RTC-A was produced in both incubations with the same retention times compared to the standard (Supplementary Fig. 6b and 6c). Additionally, MucABC-mediated reverse conversion of RTC-A back to preRTC-A was observed, indicating that the C–C bond formed by MucABC is cleavable by the enzyme, thereby enabling RTC-A to serve as an acetyl donor in a transacetylation reaction (Supplementary Fig. 7). Collectively, these findings establish that MucABC from S. macacae functions as an acyltransferase (hereafter termed SmaATase) that catalyzes C3-acetylation of preRTC-A, thereby expanding the family of acyltransferases capable of mediating non-canonical Friedel-Crafts acylation.

Acetyl-CoA serves as acetyl donor for SmaATase and PpATase

Although various phenyl esters and thioesters have been employed as acetyl donors in in vitro assays of PpATase19,21,22, its physiological acetyl donor has remained unknown. To identify a biologically relevant donor for SmaATase, we evaluated several endogenous acyl donors, including acetyl-CoA, malonyl-CoA, acetoacetyl-CoA, and acetyl-phosphate. Intriguingly, RTC-A formation was clearly observed in the presence of acetyl-CoA, whereas no signal was observed with acetyl-P and trace signals were detected with either acetoacetyl-CoA or malonyl-CoA (Fig. 1b). To determine whether this feature extends to PpATase, we expressed and purified PhlACB using the same strategy as employed for SmaATase (Supplementary Fig. 8a and b). Consistent with the results for SmaATase, reactions containing PpATase and PG yielded both MAPG and DAPG when acetyl-CoA was supplied as the donor, with only trace-level signals were detected when acetoacetyl-CoA or malonyl-CoA were used as alternative donors (Supplementary Fig. 8c). The identity of DAPG was confirmed by co-elution with an authentic standard (Supplementary Fig. 8c), while MAPG was verified by HRMS (Supplementary Fig. 8d) and NMR spectroscopy (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 9). Together, these results support acetyl-CoA as the potential physiological acetyl donor for both SmaATase and PpATase, aligning their function with that of canonical acetyltransferases23,24.

SmaATase requires tripartite assembly for catalysis

SDS-PAGE analysis confirmed successful co-purification of all three components of the SmaATase complex purified via affinity chromatography, despite only MucB carrying a C-terminal His6-tag (Supplementary Fig. 2c). Mass spectrometry further validated the presence of MucA, MucB, and MucC units in the enzyme solution, with experimentally determined masses matching theoretical predictions (Supplementary Fig. 10a). Size-exclusion chromatography indicated enzyme complex formation by showing a peak corresponding to approximately 400–600 kDa (Supplementary Fig. 10b). To determine the structural basis of SmaATase function, we resolved its cryo-EM structure at 2.32 Å resolution, revealing a dodecameric architecture composed of four MucA, four MucB, and four MucC units (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Table 3, Supplementary Figs. 11–13). This organization closely resembles the reported crystal structures of PpATase20 (Supplementary Fig. 2a) and the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex14 (Fig. 1a). In addition to the dodecamer, we observed an alternative octameric assembly (2.16 Å resolution), consisting of a MucA4 and two MucB units (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Table 3, Supplementary Figs. 11–13). Structural superposition of the dodecameric and octameric forms revealed a root-mean-square deviations (RMSD) of 0.160 Å over 2254 superposed Cα atoms, with active sites displaying comparable configuration (Supplementary Fig. 14). Furthermore, native mass spectrometry revealed additional oligomeric species (Fig. 2c), including 11-mer (MucA4B3C4), 10-mer (MucA4B2C4), 9-mer (MucA4BC4), and 8-mer (MucA4C4). These findings were corroborated by native gel electrophoresis (Supplementary Fig. 15a), indicating that SmaATase exists as a heterogeneous mixture of assemblies under the in vitro conditions tested.

Similar heterogeneity was observed for PpATase, which was previously characterized as a 12-mer [PhlA4C4B4] by crystallography20. Additional 10-mer (PhlA4C2B4) and 8-mer (PhlA4B4) were detected by native mass spectrometry (Supplementary Fig. 15b), consistent with the three distinct bands observed by native PAGE (Supplementary Fig. 15a). Quantitative mass photometry analysis revealed their relative distribution as ~4:4:2 (8-mer:10-mer:12-mer, Supplementary Fig. 15c).

To assess the requirement for complex formation in catalytic activity, we co-expressed pairwise combinations of MucA, MucB, and MucC in E. coli. Co-expression of MucAB or MucBC yielded poorly soluble proteins (Supplementary Fig. 16a and b), and purified MucAC lacked detectable C-acetylation activity (Supplementary Fig. 16c and d). Given that previous studies implicated residues within the PhlC (ACAT) subunit are essential for catalysis in PpATase20,25, we evaluated the potential of MucB (the SmaATase ortholog of PhlC) to function independently. However, the individual expression of MucB in E. coli resulted in insoluble aggregates (Supplementary Fig. 17a). Although fusion to an N-terminal trigger factor (TF) improved solubility and enabled purification (Supplementary Fig. 17a), neither TF-tagged nor cleaved MucB displayed detectable C-acetyltransferase activity (Supplementary Fig. 17b and c). Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) showed that both the full SmaATase complex (KD = 2.52 × 10⁻⁶ M) and the isolated MucB subunit (KD = 6.04 × 10⁻⁶ M) are capable of binding the substrate, with the intact complex exhibiting slightly higher affinity (Supplementary Fig. 18a). However, because the catalytic pocket of MucB is situated at the interface with MucA and MucC (Supplementary Fig. 18b), and given that individual subunits of the related archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex are either insoluble (ACAT) or inactive (HMGS) when expressed alone14, we hypothesize that MucA and MucC help constrain MucB into a catalytically competent conformation.

Structural comparison of HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complexes

Despite low sequence identity and distinct catalytic functions, SmaATase shares striking structural similarity with both PpATase and the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex at multiple levels. First, in addition to their shared dodecameric architecture, the spatial arrangement of subunits in SmaATase closely resembles that observed in PpATase and the archaeal complex (Fig. 2d). Structural alignment of the HMGS-ACAT-DUF35 modules between SmaATase and either PpATase or the archaeal homology yields RMSD of 1.245 Å (585 Cα atoms) and 1.454 Å (363 Cα atoms), respectively, underscoring the high degree of structural conservation across these systems (Supplementary Fig. 19). Second, the DUF35 subunit architecture and positioning are also conserved. MucC, a family member of DUF35 protein, features an N-terminal rubredoxin-like zinc ribbon (Supplementary Fig. 20) and a C-terminal oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide-binding (OB) fold domain. Within SmaATase, MucC is embedded in the multimeric assembly and establishes multiple contacts with neighboring MucA and MucB subunits (Supplementary Fig. 21). This arrangement resembles that of PhlB in PpATase, which bridges PhlA and PhlC, as well as the DUF35 homolog in the archaeal complex that connects the core HMGS and ACAT units (Fig. 2e). Finally, conservation is observed in the thiolase fold and the CoA-binding chamber. Both MucA and MucB adopt a conserved five-layered αβαβα core architecture characteristic of thiolase superfamily enzymes (Supplementary Fig. 22)11,26. This structural signature is also preserved in PhlA and PhlC of PpATase and the HMGS and ACAT units of the archaeal complex (Supplementary Fig. 22). Additionally, a hallmark of the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex is the presence of a fused CoA-binding site at the HMGS–ACAT interface, which facilitates shuttling of the pantetheinyl arm between active sites during catalysis (Fig. 2f). Notably, a similar interfacial chamber is retained in both SmaATase and PpATase (Fig. 2f, supplementary Fig. 23), despite the absence of the HDxF motif in the thiolase domains and the key Claisen condensation residues in the HMGS units (details will be discussed in the following section).

Together, these structural observations indicate that the HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex represents a deeply conserved architectural module that may have been evolutionarily repurposed from primary metabolism to secondary metabolism.

Key catalytic residue mutations support functional divergence

Given the striking structural conservation of archaeal and bacterial HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complexes as acetyl-CoA-utilizing C-acetyltransferases, we conducted a phylogenetic analysis comparing their ACAT and HMGS units with representative members of the thiolase superfamily to elucidate the evolutionary origins of SmaATase and PpATase. As expected, enzymes are clustered according to their functions (Fig. 3a). MucA/PhlA and their homologs formed a clade closely related to archaeal HMGSs, while MucB/PhlC and their homologs grouped near archaeal ACATs (Fig. 3a), supporting their evolutionary relationship with the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex involved in mevalonate biosynthesis. Beyond the αβαβα structural motif, a hallmark of the thiolase superfamily is a catalytic cysteine (Cys) residue that mediates CoA or acyl carrier protein (ACP) substrate attachment27. However, multiple sequence alignment revealed the absence of the typical E-C-H-N tetrad conserved among HMGSs in MucA/PhlA and related sequences (Fig. 3b). Similarly, although MucB/PhlC and their homologs retain the CxS and GHx motifs characteristic of ACATs, they lack the HDxF motif present in archaeal ACATs (Fig. 3b). These sequence deviations likely contribute to the functional divergence of bacterial HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complexes from their archaeal counterparts.

To test the functional significance of these divergent residues, we first assessed whether SmaATase and PpATase could catalyze the Claisen condensation of acetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA. LC-MS analysis revealed the formation of CoA, but not HMG-CoA, from incubations with either enzyme (Fig. 3c), indicating that both utilize acetyl-CoA solely as a donor. To further validate this, we prepared the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex using the same purification protocols and generated two variants: one carrying an H284A substitution in the ACAT unit’s HDxF motif, and another with substitutions in the HMGS unit’s E-C-H-N catalytic tetrad entirely (Supplementary Fig. 24). While the wild-type complex produced HMG-CoA from acetyl-CoA, neither mutant yielded detectable product (Fig. 3c), confirming the essentiality of these residues for canonical HMGS activity.

To gain deeper insights into the sequence diversity of SmaATase-like enzyme complexes, we mined bacterial genomes in the NCBI database and identified 1,030 BGCs containing co-localized HMGS, ACAT, and DUF35 genes (Fig. 4a). The vast majority of the identified BGCs (1,001) lacked adjacent biosynthetic machinery for canonical secondary metabolism, only 29 BGCs were predicted to be associated with secondary metabolism (Fig. 4b). These include muc-like clusters from Streptococcus species, featuring hybrid NRPS-PKS assembly lines, and phl-like clusters from Pseudomonas species harboring type III PKSs (Fig. 4b).

Given the dominance of this uncharacterized category, and its lack of obvious biosynthetic partners, we next asked whether these minimal HMGS–ACAT–DUF35 loci might encode functionally distinct or evolutionarily intermediate enzyme complexes. To explore this possibility, we selected a representative candidate from Pseudomonas fluorescens for further analysis. This PfACAT/HMGS-DUF35 complex features a fused HMGS-DUF35 protein and, importantly, lacks any neighboring PKS or NRPS genes (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Figs. 25 and 26). Sequence alignment showed that its HMGS domain lacks the E-C-H-N tetrad, whereas its ACAT unit retains the catalytic Cys and conserved HDxF and GHx motifs (Fig. 3b), suggesting that the HMGS unit is inactive whereas the ACAT component remains functionally intact.

In vitro biochemical assays confirmed this functional divergence: the PfACAT/HMGS-DUF35 complex did not produce HMG-CoA or acetoacetyl-CoA from acetyl-CoA, resembling SmaATase and PpATase (Fig. 3c). In contrast, it catalyzed the thiolytic cleavage of acetoacetyl-CoA to generate acetyl-CoA, a reaction not observed for SmaATase and PpATase (Fig. 4c). Introducing an H294Y mutation in PfACAT nearly abolished this activity (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 25), confirming the essential catalytic role of the His residue within the HDxF motif. This finding is consistent with observations in Geobacter metallireducens BbsAB, a DUF35-associated sterol-carrier-protein (SCP2)-type thiolase where the HDxF motif mediates reversible benzylsuccinyl-CoA formation from benzoyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA28.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the PfACAT/HMGS-DUF35 complex may represent an evolutionary intermediate that has lost its primary metabolic function but has not yet been recruited into a defined specialized pathway. In contrast, SmaATase and PpATase have undergone further evolution, characterized by the loss of the HDxF motif and remodeling of the active-site architectures within the ACAT domain that enables specific recognition of small-molecule acetyl acceptors (Fig. 5). To elucidate the substrate-binding mode of SmaATase, we performed molecular docking and dynamics simulations (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 27). A comparison with the well-established catalytic mechanism of PpATase20,25 reveals that key catalytic residues are largely conserved: the catalytic nucleophile (Cys88 in PhlC vs Cys87 in MucB); the general base (Glu116 vs Asp115); the proton source residue and proton shuttling residues (Asp137-Thr132-His144 vs Asp136-Thr131-His143, Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 28). Notably, the catalytic cysteine is acetylated in both the PpATase20 (Cys88, 5MG5) and SmaATase (Cys87) structures; this was evidenced by residual electron density in both cases and confirmed for SmaATase by LC-MS/MS analysis (Supplementary Fig. 29).

Despite the conserved catalytic core, clear differences are observed in the substrate-binding region. For example, His56 and Tyr124 in PhlC are replaced by Ala55 and Phe123 in MucB, respectively, and the flexible lid residue Trp211 in PhlC29 is substituted by Ala210 in MucB (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 28). Sequence alignment further shows that key catalytic and substrate-binding residues are well conserved within PhlC or MucB homologs, yet markedly divergent from those in archaeal ACATs (Supplementary Fig. 28). Together, these observations indicate that although SmaATase and PpATase retain a shared catalytic apparatus inherited from their ancestral thiolase scaffolds, they have undergone functional repurposing through reconfiguration of their substrate-binding sites, enabling them to recognize chemically distinct acetyl acceptors.

Acetylation confers antimicrobial activity of RTC-A and DAPG

RTC-A is a tetramic acid-derived antibiotic with broad-spectrum activity against gram-positive bacteria15,30,31. To evaluate the biological relevance of the acetylation modification catalyzed by streptococcal ATases, we compared the antimicrobial activities of RTC-A and its unacetylated precursor, preRTC-A, against both oral streptococcal competitors and clinically relevant pathogens. Strikingly, RTC-A exhibited potent antibacterial effects against all tested strains, whereas preRTC-A showed negligible inhibition (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 30). A similar structure–activity relationship was observed for the DAPG/PG pair, with DAPG displayed markedly stronger antimicrobial activity than PG against most strains (with the exception of S. gordonii and S. oralis) (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 30). Together, these results establish acetylation as a critical modification for the antimicrobial potency of both RTC-A and DAPG, underscoring the ecological significance of evolved ATases from Streptococcus and Pseudomonas species in interspecies competition.
paper_content.methods:
General methods

All reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bidepharm, and Aladin. Gene synthesis, plasmid construction, and point mutation were carried out by Tsingke Biotechnology Company (Supplementary Table 4). All codon-optimized DNA and protein sequences used in this study are provided as a Source Data file. Luria-Bertani (LB, 1% NaCl, 1% tryptone, and 0.5% yeast extract) medium was used for culturing E. coli. Chloramphenicol (25 μg/mL), ampicillin (50 μg/mL), and kanamycin (50 μg/mL) were used for the selection of recombinant E. coli strains. Antibacterial activity assays were performed using indicator strains cultured in Mueller-Hinton broth (MHB, OXOID), except for S. oralis and S. gordonii, which were maintained in brain-heart infusion (BHI, OXOID) broth due to poor growth in MHB.

Protein expression and purification

Codon-optimized genes encoding SmaATase (mucABC), PpATase (phlACB), archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex, pfACAT/HMGS-DUF35 complex, and individual combinations of MucABC subunits were cloned into the pACYCDuet-1 and transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) for protein expression. Codon-optimized mucB gene was cloned into both pET28a(+) and pCold-TF (TF = trigger factor) for enhanced soluble expression. Cells harboring the expression plasmid were grown overnight in LB supplemented with appropriate antibiotic at 37 °C and 220 r.p.m. to prepare the preculture. Five milliliters of preculture were then inoculated into 500 mL of LB medium containing the same antibiotic and cultured under identical conditions. Protein expression was induced with 0.2 mM isopropyl β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) at OD600 ~0.6, followed by incubation at 30 °C (21 h, 140 rpm). For the expression of MucB, the culture was incubated at 16 °C, 160 rpm for 16 h after adding 0.2 mM IPTG. Cells were harvested and resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole, 10% glycerol, pH 8.0). The suspension was disrupted by ultrasonication (40% amplitude, 10 min, pulse 3 sec, pause 6 sec) and then centrifuged at 13,000 × g for 30 min to spin down the cell debris. Recombinant proteins were purified using an ÄKTA go system (Cytiva) equipped with HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva). Eluted proteins were buffer-exchanged into 50 mM Kpi buffer (pH 7.5) containing 10% glycerol using PD-10 desalting columns (Cytiva). Protein concentrations were determined after concentration with Amicon Ultra filters (Merck Millipore). Size-exclusion chromatography was performed using an ÄKTA go system equipped with a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) pre-equilibrated with 50 mM Kpi buffer (pH 7.5) containing 150 mM NaCl. Purity of proteins was assessed by SDS-PAGE analysis (Supplementary Fig. 32) and imaged using the GelDoc Go system (Bio-Rad). Freshly purified enzyme complexes were used for all in vitro assays to ensure activity.

Activity assays

Enzymatic assays for functional characterization of SmaATase were carried out in 100 μL reaction mixtures containing 50 mM Kpi buffer (pH 7.5), 12 μM purified enzyme, 1 mM preRTC-A, and various acetyl donors at the following concentrations: 1.5 mM PA, 25 mM N-AcIm, 10 mM IPEA (supplemented with 10 mM imidazole), 10 mM EtSAc, 1.5 mM acetyl-CoA, 1.5 mM malonyl-CoA, 1.5 mM acetoacetyl-CoA, 1.5 mM acetyl-P. Reactions were incubated at 30 °C for 16 h and quenched by the addition of 100 μL methanol. After centrifugation at 21,000 × g for 30 min, supernatants were analyzed by ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) using LC method 1 (Supplementary Table 5). UPLC was performed on an Agilent 1290 system equipped with a Phenomenex Kinetex XB-C18 column (4.6 mm × 100 mm, 2.6 μm), and data were processed using Agilent OpenLab CDS ChemStation Edition C.01.07.

For PpATase activity assays, 100 μL reaction mixtures contained 50 mM Kpi buffer (pH 7.5), 12 μM purified enzyme, 1 mM PG, 1.5 mM of either PA, or acetyl-CoA, malonyl-CoA, acetoacetyl-CoA, acetyl-P. Reactions were incubated at 30 °C for 16 h, and quenched with 100 μL methanol, and centrifuged at 21,000 × g for 30 min. Supernatants were analyzed by UPLC using LC method 2 (Supplementary Table 5).

For in vitro HMG-CoA formation assays, 50 μL reaction mixtures were prepared containing 50 mM Kpi buffer (pH 7.5), 15 μM purified enzyme, 1 mM acetyl-CoA, and 1 mM CoA. After incubation at 30 °C for 2.5 h, reactions were quenched with 2.5 μL formic acid and 50 μL methanol. Samples were centrifuged at 21,000 × g for 30 min, and supernatants were analyzed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) using LC method 3 (Supplementary Table 5). Thiolytic cleavage activity of acetoacetyl-CoA was assessed in 50 μL reaction mixtures containing 50 mM Kpi buffer (pH 7.5), 15 μM purified enzyme, 1 mM acetoacetyl-CoA, and 1 mM CoA. After incubation at 30 °C for 30 min, reactions were quenched with 2.5 μL formic acid and 50 μL methanol. Following centrifugation (21,000 × g, 30 min), supernatants were analyzed by LC-MS using LC method 4 (Supplementary Table 5) on a Phenomenex Kinetex XB-C18 column (4.6 mm × 100 mm, 2.6 μm).

All LC-MS analyses were performed on the 1290 infinity UPLC system coupled to an Agilent Technologies 6470 triple quadrupole mass spectrometer. The LC/TQ used a Jet Stream Electrospray Ionization (AJS-ESI) source operated in the negative ionization mode (capillary voltage, 3.5 kV; gas temperature, 300 °C; drying gas, 5 L·min-1; fragmentor voltage: 135 V; nebulizer, 45 psig; sheath gas flow, 11 L·min-1; acquisition range, 100–1500 m/z). MS data were processed using Agilent MassHunter Qualitative Analysis B.06.00.

Isolation and characterization of the enzymatic products

To determine the structure of the enzymatic product of SmaATase, the in vitro reaction was scaled up to 50 mL reaction volume containing 50 mM Kpi buffer (pH 7.5), 1 mM preRTC-A, 1.5 mM PA, 15 μM purified enzyme, and incubated at 30 °C for 16 h. For MAPG isolation, the reaction was similarly scaled up to 100 mL using 1 mM PG and the same buffer and enzyme conditions, followed by incubation at 30 °C for 16 h. Reaction mixtures were extracted three times with equal volume of ethyl acetate (EtOAc), and the organic phases were combined and concentrated under vacuum. RTC-A (tR = 10.6 min) was purified via semi-preparative HPLC on a Phenomenex Kinetex XB-C column (250 mm × 10 mm, 5 μm) using isocratic elution with acetonitrile (ACN)/H2O (95:5, v/v) containing 0.1% TFA at a flow rate of 2.5 mL/min. MAPG (tR = 6.9 min) was purified under similar conditions using ACN/H2O (40:60, v/v) with 0.1% TFA. The 1H and 13C NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker Advance Neo 400 MHz or 600 MHz spectrometer and processed by MestReNova 6.1.0 (Metrelab). NMR data are presented in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2, and NMR spectra are provided in Supplementary Figs. 4, 5, 7, and 9.

Cryo-EM structural determination

For Cryo-EM sample preparation, Holey carbon grids (Au R1.2/1.3, 300 mesh, Quantifoil) were used with 30 s glow-discharge using medium power of Plasma Cleaner PDC-32G (Harrick). The Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was maintained at the conditions of 8 °C and 100% humidity during sample preparation. For each sample, 3.5 μL of protein (3.8 mg/mL of SmaATase in 50 mM potassium phosphate, pH 7.5) were loaded on the grid, blotted for 4.5 s with filter paper, and plunged into liquid ethane. The vitrified grids were subsequently transferred to liquid nitrogen for storage.

Data acquisition was performed on the 300 kV Titan Krios electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a Falcon 4i detector and GIF Quantum energy filter. A total of 3089 micrographs were collected automatically using EPU, with a preset defocus range of −1.2 to −1.8 μm. Each image stack received a total dose of 50 e-/Å², and the final images were binned to a pixel size of 0.927 Å.

Data processing flow shown in Supplementary Fig. 11 was performed on cryoSPARC v4.7. Initial particle picking using blob picking yielded 1,155,067 particles. Following 2D classification, 973,419 particles were retained and re-extracted at bin 1 for subsequent processing. Ab-initio reconstruction of these particles produced an octameric structure, and the resolution of this structure reaches 2.16 Å after non-uniform refinement. During 2D classification, we observed particles exhibiting higher-order polymeric assemblies. Through iterative ab-initio reconstruction and 3D classification, we isolated 71,520 particles for subsequent processing. Non-uniform refinement followed by local refinement of these particles yielded a dodecameric structure at 2.32 Å resolution.

Structural models for the octameric and dodecameric complexes were built based on their respective cryo-EM maps. The initial monomeric models of MucA, MucB, and MucC, predicted by AlphaFold2, were docked into the density maps using ChimeraX to generate initial complex models. These models were then manually adjusted and refined in Coot, followed by automated real-space refinement using phenix.real_space_refine in PHENIX. The stereochemical quality of the final models was validated with MolProbity. Data collection and refinement statistics are summarized in Table S3. The atomic coordinates and structure factors have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank under accession codes 9VBO (octamer) and 9VBT (dodecamer).

Mass spectrometry

For TOF mass spectrometry, SmaATase (n = 3) was buffered to 50 mM ammonium acetate (pH 7.5) before applying on SYNAPT XS (Waters) mass spectrometer equipped with an ACQUITY UPLC I-Class PLUS system. A 2 μL aliquot of protein solution (1 mg/mL) was injected onto a MAbPacTM RP column (3.0 mm × 100 mm, 4 μm, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and separated using LC method 5 (Supplementary Table 5). Mass spectrometry was performed on a Waters SYNAPT XS operating in positive ESI mode over the range of 200−4000 m/z.

Chromatography-coupled mass spectrometry was performed at 1 mm scale with the following optimized conditions: Electrospray voltage: 3.0 kV, ion source: 120 °C, desolvation: 450 °C, cone gas: 50 L/h, desolvation gas: 800 L/h, nebulizer pressure: 6.5 bar. Raw spectra were acquired using MassLynx 4.2 (Waters) and processed through Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) deconvolution to generate the molecular mass spectra of injected proteins.

Native MS analysis was performed using a Q-Exactive Plus Hybrid Quadrupole-Orbitrap Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Samples (n = 3) were buffer-exchanged into 0.2 M ammonium acetate (pH 7.5) and loaded on a gold-coated capillary installed on a nESI source. Spectra were acquired with 1.4 kV spray voltage, 20 ms maximum inject time, and 50−200 V collisional activation in the HCD cell. Mass and charge assignments were determined using an Excel script kindly provided by the Benesch Laboratory, University of Oxford.

For protein posttranslational modification analysis, SmaATase (n = 3; 2.5 mg/mL in 50 mM Kpi buffer, pH = 7.5) were reduced with TCEP [Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine, 10 mM] at 37 °C with agitation (800 rpm) for 60 min, alkylated with iodoacetamide (IAA, 40 mM) in the dark at room temperature for 30 min, and digested in-solution with a combination of trypsin and chymotrypsin, both at a ratio of 1:50 (w/w) to SmaATase, in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate at 37 °C for overnight. The digestion was quenched with 0.1% formic acid, and the resulting peptides were desalted prior to LC-MS/MS analysis. Approximately 1 μg of sample was injected into a Vanquish Neo nanoflow LC system equipped with a Orbitrap Exploris 480 Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were separated on an Acclaim PepMap 100 C18 column (250 mm × 75 μm, 3 μm, Thermo Fisher Scientific) by using LC method 6 (Supplementary Table 5). Full-scan MS spectra (m/z 350–1500) were acquired in the Orbitrap in DDA mode at a resolution of 120,000 (at m/z 200), with an RF lens setting of 50%, an automatic gain control (AGC) target of 300%, and a max IT of 25 ms. MS/MS analysis was performed with the following settings: MS2 resolution of 15,000 (at m/z 200); the AGC target was set to 200% and the max IT to 22 ms; dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s; MS2 scan range was set to m/z 150–2000. The most intense ions fulfilling the predefined criteria were isolated with a 1.6 Th window and fragmented via higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) with a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 28%. The cycle time was 2 s, the dynamic exclusion duration was 30 s, and all other parameters were set to default values. Database searching was performed using Peaks Studio 13 software. The mass error tolerances were set to 10 ppm for precursor ions and 0.02 Da for fragment ions; enzyme specificity was set to semi-specific for both trypsin and chymotrypsin, allowing for a maximum of two missed cleavages and a minimum of 6 amino acid residues for the peptide sequence length. Protease cleavage sites were defined for trypsin and chymotrypsin at lysine (K) and arginine (R) residues. The following variable modifications were included in the search: Oxidation (M: +15.9949 Da); Acetylation (C: +42.0106 Da); Acetylation (Protein N-terminus: +42.0106 Da); Carbamidomethylation (+57.0215 Da); Carboxymethylation (+58.0055 Da). Filter parameters were set as follows: PSM -10LgP ≥ 20.0, Proteins -10LgP ≥ 15.0. PTM localization was assessed using an Ascore threshold of 15, and a minimum of one unique peptide was required for protein identification.

Mass photometry measurements

Protein samples were diluted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to a final concentration of 200 nM for mass photometry analysis. Measurements were performed on a OneMP instrument (Refeyn) using pre-cleaned glass coverslips. Following the standard protocol, 10 μL of PBS was loaded into the sample well for system focusing, followed by the addition of 10 μL diluted protein sample (1:1 mixing ratio). Data acquisition commenced immediately after mixing, recording for 60 s at 100 frames/s using AcquireMP software v2.3. The system was calibrated with bovine serum albumin (BSA) standards. Raw data were processed using DiscoverMP software v2.1.

Phylogenetic analysis

Protein sequences of thiolase superfamily members were compiled from published datasets. Homologs of MucA, MucB, PhlA, and PhlC were obtained via BLASTP searches against the NCBI non-redundant protein database (nr). All sequences used in the analysis are provided as a Source Data file. Multiple sequence alignments were performed using MUSCLE with default parameters. Phylogenetic reconstruction was conducted in MEGA 11 using the Neighbour-Joining method with the Poisson model, incorporating 500 bootstrap replicates to assess node support. The resulting Newick-formatted tree was visualized using the Interactive Tree of Life (iTOL) server tool (https://itol.embl.de/).

Genome mining methods

To systematically identify multi-component enzyme complexes with C-acyltransferase activity across the bacterial kingdom, a domain-centric genome mining approach was employed. Based on the biosynthetic gene cluster organization of muc and phl BGC, hidden Markov model (HMM) search were conducted for Pfam domain corresponding to HMGS (MucA and PhlA), ACAT (MucB and PhlC), DUF35 proteins (MucC and PhlB). Specifically, the domains corresponding to PF08541 [3-oxoacyl-(acyl-carrier-protein) synthase III C-terminal], PF00108 (thiolase), and PF01796 (DUF35 OB-fold domain), respectively, served as probes for further genome mining. The thiolase domain was used as the anchor, and genomic regions encompassing 10 genes upstream and downstream were scanned for the presence of the other two domains. Loci containing all three domains were retained, and redundancy was eliminated using FastANI. The resulting BGCs were analyzed using antiSMASH and visualized with BiG-SCAPE.

Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation

The ligand structure was first optimized at the B3LYP/def2-TZVP level of theory using the ORCA 5.0.4 quantum chemistry package to obtain a reliable equilibrium geometry and electronic structure. The optimized ligand was subsequently docked into the target protein using the DiffDock. The top-ranked docking pose, based on DiffDock’s confidence score and binding-site complementarity, was selected for further molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Docking poses were visualized using PyMOL v3.0 and ProLIF.

To investigate the interaction between the ligand and the MucA-B-C protein complex, classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out. In the constructed systems, the protonation states of all ionizable residues were determined using PROPKA, based on empirical pKa predictions under physiological pH conditions. The following residues were modeled in their protonated form: His305 and Asp35 in MucA; Glu57, Asp134, and Glu296 in MucB; and Glu70 in MucC. All remaining residues retained their standard protonation states at neutral pH. All MD simulations were performed with GROMACS (version 2025.03) using an all-atom force field for the protein (AMBER ff14SB) and a compatible ligand topology generated via appropriate parameterization (GAFF2). RESP charges were generated using Psi4 for all ligands as well as for the acetylated Cys87 residue. The protein–ligand complex was solvated in a cubic box with explicit TIP3P water molecules, and counter ions (Na⁺/Cl⁻) were added to neutralize the total charge.

Prior to dynamics, the system underwent energy minimization using the steepest descent algorithm until the maximum force fell below 1000 kJ·mol⁻¹·nm⁻¹, ensuring removal of steric clashes. Subsequently, two equilibration phases were performed: The system was equilibrated for 1 ns under the canonical ensemble using the V-rescale thermostat to maintain the temperature at 300 K, while restraining the heavy atoms of the protein and ligand with a force constant of 1000 kJ·mol⁻¹·nm⁻¹. The simulation was continued for 1 ns under the isothermal–isobaric ensemble (NPT), maintaining a pressure of 1 bar using the Parrinello–Rahman barostat. Position restraints were retained to allow solvent and ions to relax around the solute. Finally, to improve statistical sampling, three independent 200 ns production MD simulations were conducted in the NPT ensemble without positional restraints, starting from distinct randomized initial velocity distributions. A 2 fs integration time step was employed, and all covalent bonds involving hydrogen atoms were constrained using the LINCS algorithm. Long-range electrostatic interactions were treated with the Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method, and van der Waals interactions were truncated at 1.0 nm. Trajectories were saved every 10 ps for subsequent analyses. The binding free energy between the ligand and protein was calculated using the MM/GBSA method.

Antibacterial activity and MIC assays

Stock solutions of preRTC-A, RTC-A, PG, and DAPG were prepared in DMSO at concentrations of 6.4 mg/mL or 8 mg/mL. Ampicillin sodium salt, dissolved in water at the same concentrations, served as a positive control. The following indicator strains were used: Streptococcus salivarius DA547, Streptococcus oralis DA1241, Streptococcus gordonii ATCC10558, Bacillus subtilis 168, Staphylococcus aureus ATCC29213, Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus 544, Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus 103 and Streptococcus pneumonia ATCC49619. For MIC assays, compounds were serially 2-fold diluted in MHB to 50 μL per well in 96-well plates. Bacterial cultures in mid-log phase were diluted to 1 × 106 CFU/mL in MHB, and 50 μL of this suspension was added to each well, yielding a final inoculum of 5 × 105 CFU/mL (validated range: 2 × 105 CFU/mL to 8 × 105 CFU/mL). Streptococcus oralis DA1241 and S. gordonii ATCC10558 were cultured in BHI due to poor growth in MHB. Each plate included antimicrobial-free medium as a negative control and untreated bacterial culture as a growth control. Plates were incubated at 37 °C for 18 h, and absorbance was measured at 625 nm using a BioTek Epoch 2 (Agilent). MIC values were defined as the lowest concentration that completely inhibited visible growth (OD625 ≤ 0.02 compared to the negative control). All assays were performed in duplicate and independently repeated three times.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In their manuscript, Liao et al study bacterial tripartite complex systems analogous to the thiolase/HMG-CoA synthase/DUF-35 protein used by archaea to catalyse the first steps of isoprenoid synthesis. Through an impressive panel of methods ranging from enzymology, structural biology, biochemistry, bioinformatics, phylogeny, and even genome mining, they found that the thiolase subunit from the bacterial homologues from Streptomyces macacae (SmaATase) and from Pseudomonas protegens (PpATase) catalyse a rare Friedel-Crafts reaction involving acetyl-CoA as acetyl donor. The end products of these reactions ultimately generate molecules with antibiotic activities. It is without any doubt a study of high quality, bringing to light an enzymatic complex involved in secondary metabolism that most probably originates from a central carbon metabolism involved in isoprenoid biosynthesis. The reviewer congratulates the authors on this excellent study that reaches the standard of Nature Communications, and would strongly support its publication upon addressing these minor comments.
1- Abstract: “Cryo-electron microscopy of the S. macaca-derived thiolase complex”.
Shouldn´t it be S. macacae instead of S. macaca?
2- Title of the result first subsection. “Characterization of Streptococcal ATases as non-canonical Friedel-Crafts acylases”. For clarification, it would be helpful to state the meaning of “ATases” here or before instead of using the abbreviation. Moreover, since the physiological donor is acetyl-CoA, authors should consider using the term acetylases instead of acylases.
3- Legend of Supplementary Fig. 2c. “SDS-PAGE analysis of the heterologous expression and purification results of SmaATase, SmuATase, and StrATase, respectively. SmaATase, SmuATase, and StrATase represent MucABC enzyme complex from S. mutans, S. macacae, S. troglodytae, respectively.”
Based on the text and results, it should be: “SDS-PAGE analysis of the heterologous expression and purification results of SmaATase, SmuATase, and StrATase, respectively. SmaATase, SmuATase, and StrATase represent MucABC enzyme complex from S. macacae, S. mutans, S. troglodytae, respectively.”
4- 2nd paragraph results: “Additionally, MucABC-mediated reverse conversion of RTC-A back to preRTC-A was observed, confirming the bidirectionality of the reaction (Supplementary Fig. 6d).” Would it be possible to provide the Standard Gibbs free energy for the reaction? That would provide some insights on its expected directionality.
5- 3rd paragraph results: “Notably, earlier studies reported no detectable product formation when PpATase was incubated with acetyl-CoA”. By curiosity, do the authors have an explanation for why the activity was not observable before with acetyl-CoA?
6- Supplementary Fig. 9. Please define “Cald.” in the legend. Could the authors explain the differences between observed and calculated masses for MucB and MucA (e.g., 44481 Da versus 44351 Da)?
7- Supplementary Fig. 10. Has the mask used to generate the local refinement been deposited in the EMDB? Adding an extra panel with the mask on Fig. S10 would be informative and provide more transparency on the model-building process. Moreover, for Figures S10 and S11, is the map based on raw data or a sharpened one? This should be stated in the legend.
8- Figure 2. According to the legend, panels d and e must be swapped.
9- 4th paragraph results: “In addition to the dodecamer, we observed an alternative octameric assembly (2.16 Å resolution), consisting of a MucA4C4 core”. The nomenclature seems wrong and should be MucA4C2 according to the deposited model.
10- 4th paragraph results: “Structural superposition of the dodecameric and octameric forms revealed a root-mean-square deviations (r.m.s.d.) of 0.173 Å”. Please add the number of superposed Calpha.
11- 4th paragraph results: “…indicating that SmaATase exists as a heterogeneous mixture of assemblies under near-physiological conditions.”. This is a very dangerous statement that must be reformulated because the tested conditions in vitro are expected to be very different compared to the physiological ones (molecular crowding, physicochemical conditions, protein concentrations…). Rather, use “under in vitro conditions” or “in solution”.
12- 7th paragraph results: “Structural alignment of the HMGS-ACAT-DUF35 modules between SmaATase and either PpATase or the archaeal homolog yields r.m.s.d. of 1.245 Å and 1.466 Å,” Please add the number of superposed Calpha.
13- 7th paragraph results: “DUF35 subunit architecture and positioning: MucC, a family member of DUF35 protein, features an N-terminal rubredoxin-like zinc ribbon and a C-terminal oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide-binding (OB) fold domain.”. IMPORTANT POINT. Unfortunately, MucC has been modelled without the 4 conserved Cys binding the Zn. The Zn is observable in the EM map together with the four Cys binding to it. See the attached picture.
Zn has been modelled in all structural homologues, and must be modelled in both structures from this work. Presenting an additional supplementary figure with a close-up of the Zn binding site and the electron density would be informative.
Moreover, Cys87 in ACAT subunit of SmaATase could be acetylated. Mass spectrometry might provide some clues if this residue is truly acetylated in the protein in solution (e.g., with the acetyl-group coming from acetyl-CoA from E. coli). Based on the electron density, there is high suspicion that Cys87 is indeed acetylated. Therefore, the referee suggests adding an acetyl group on this cysteine (as it has been done for PpATase structure), and if possible, obtain a confirmation by mass spectrometry. Presenting an additional supplementary figure with a close-up of the acetylated Cys87 and the electron density would be informative. If mass spectrometry, or author´s conclusions point to a non-acetylated form, please add a snapshot of the Cys87 with the surrounding electron density for each chain.
To conclude on the model, the referee would suggest adding the Zn, the acetyl group and polishing the model further for a better fit in the electron density. For instance, some loops and sidechains are observable in the electron density, but were not modelled (see below). Please correct the residue presenting a very high clash score (higher than 0.8).
14- Supplementary Fig. 17. Presented residues should be labelled. A second snapshot with a 90° orientation could be useful to show the different residues. Also, hydrogen bond distances are impossible to read. Please remove the distances label, keep the dashes (in another colour than yellow) and add a general statement such as: all hydrogen bond distances below 3.5 Å are displayed as dashes.
15- 7th paragraph results: “). Additionally, a hallmark of the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex is the presence of a fused CoA-binding site at the HMGS–ACAT interface, which facilitates shuttling of the pantetheinyl arm between active sites during catalysis (Fig. 2f).”
A supplementary figure comparing the CoA binding site between the archaeal ACAT/HMGS/DUF-35 protein (PDB 6ESQ) and SmaATase would reinforce the observation made on Fig. 2f. Are most of the residues conserved? Also, please correct the typo on Fig. 2f “fused Co-A binding” should be “fused CoA-binding”.
16- 11th paragraph results: “Introducing an H294Y mutation in PfACAT nearly abolished this activity (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 20), confirming the essential catalytic role of the His residue within the HDxF motif.”. This is a very interesting point. Are the authors expecting a role in antibiotic biosynthesis for this enzyme? It is unlikely that its physiological function would be simply the formation of acetyl-CoA from acetoacetyl-CoA. The latter might simply be a side reaction.
17- Figure 5: Cys88 is acetylated, please label the residue accordingly (e.g., Acetyl-C88). D137 cited in the text is not shown on the figure. Importantly, the difference in the active site pose confuses the reader as it seems that the orientation between PpATase and SmaATase is the same, but the position of the residues (particularly C88/H347 and C87/H349) is different. Please take a new picture with the exact same orientation between PpATase and SmaATase active sites. Highlight the key residues C88/H347 and C87/H349 with a bold label.
18- Supplementary Fig. 23: Why is the hydrogen bond not shown for Q302? Is there a possibility to switch the H143 rotamer to gain a hydrogen bond with the ligand without generating steric clashes? Here, 4.1 A seems too distant for efficient
19- Supplementary Fig. 24: The final concentration of the used compounds must be stated in the figure or legend.
20- Last paragraph of the result section: “Although preRTC-A showed modest activity against S. gordonii ATCC 10558 (MIC = 32 μg/mL), RTC-A demonstrated a 32-fold enhancement in potency (MIC = 1 μg/mL; Fig. 6). A similar trend was observed for the phenolic polyketide DAPG and its biosynthetic precursor PG. DAPG exhibited significantly higher antimicrobial activity against most tested strains (except S. oralis DA1241 and S. gordonii ATCC 10558) compared to PG, recapitulating the structure–activity relationship observed for RTC-A and preRTC-A pair (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 24).”. The whole sentence should be clarified. The results obtained are excellent, and authors should rather use a general statement to describe the results, for instance: All strains showed inhibition for DAPG compared to PG, except S. gordonii and S. oralis. The effect is even more pronounced for preRTC-A versus RTC-A, where all tested strains showed inhibition for RTA-A compared to preRTC-A.”
21- 1st paragraph discussion: “In contrast, SmaATase is remarkable for its ability to catalyze Friedel–Crafts acylation independently of CoA or ACP-activated acyl donors, highlighting its potential as a versatile biocatalyst for synthetic applications.” The acetylation is CoA-dependent. Please rephrase.
22- 2nd paragraph discussion: “…enzyme complexes in secondary metabolism are more commonly associated with scaffold formation (such as PKS37 and NRPS38) than with structural modification”. What is the meaning of structural modification here? Please reformulate.
23- Supplementary Fig. 25: It would help the reader to add the acetylated cysteine residue position in the three studied systems (in the figure or in the legend).
24- Methods, protein expression and purification: “and imaged using the DelDoc Go system (Bio-Rad).”. It should be GelDoc Go system.
25- Methods, Cryo-EM structural determination: Please provide the following information.
Protein concentration and buffer used for the grid.
How did authors build, refine, and validate the model?
“Ab-initio reconstruction of these particles produced an octameric structure at 2.16 Å resolution.” Ab initio is not a refinement technique, so it does not make sense to associate ab initio with resolution. Please reformulate.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Xiaoyu Tang and colleagues present a manuscript detailing the biochemical characterization of a tripartite enzymatic complex catalyzing Friedel-Crafts-Acylation in the biosynthesis of the antibiotic tetramate reutericyclin A. This enzymatic complex bears similarities to a previously characterized system able to catalyze acetylation of phloroglucinol. The protein complex was structurally characterized via Cryo-EM, revealing a dodecameric structure, analogous to a previously characterized pathway in archaeal mevalonate biosynthesis. Bioinformatic analyses showed that key catalytic residues of the primary metabolism enzyme were lost, and new, potentially critical residues for a new catalytic functon(acetylation) acquired. Based on these findings, the authors pose the hypothesis that the enzymatic complex was repurposed during evolution to acquire a new catalytic function. Finally, the authors show that acetylation is an essential feature for antibiotic activity in both reutericyclins and phloroglucinols, highlighting the biological importance of this modification.
The paper is very well and clearly written and contains a lot of data. The experiments were carried out with a range of state-of the-art methodologies, and the results are nicely presented in main and SI Figures. Overall, this study deserves publication in Nature Communications. However, there are a couple of issues that should be improved or taken care of before publication:
Major:
l.265: SmaATase is praised having potential as a “versatile biocatalyst for synthetic applications.” Indeed, the possible use of different acetyl donors has been demonstrated, but the substrate scope has not been investigated at all to my understanding, except for the acetylation of the native substrate pre-RTC and its short chain analogue. Of course, a comprehensive enzymatic study is beyond the scope of this paper, but it would be nice to provide some initial characterization: e.g. on simplified pyrrolidones with a few different substituents. Also, I wonder, if propionyl chains could be accepted?
Figure 3b: The loss of key catalytic residues of primary metabolic enzymes has been shown, but I am missing a Figure, where the acquisition of key residues for the new catalytic functon(see Figure 5, Fig. S23) is analyzed. It would be good to provide a similar Figure and underlying alignments for these residues in primary vs. secondary metabolism. Do all 31 enzymes contain the same sequence motifs in this region or are there variations?
Figure 4b,c and corresponding main text l.218-230: This part is not entirely clear to me: The first sentence “While no other function predictable Friedel–Crafts acylases were identified” makes no sense to me. Also, to me it is not clear, why the enzyme from P. fluorescens was selected for further analysis. The rationale behind this experiment should be better explained, as well the meaning of the obtained results.
Minor:
Methods: In the genome mining section, a reference for BiG-SCAPE should be added.
Fig. 3a: Why are MucC/PhlB homologues not included in the phylogenetic tree?
Fig. S7: What is the meaning of PA in this Figure?
Fig: S24: The photos are barely visible and recognizable. Please improve Figure quality.
Fig. S26: In this Figure, it is referred to proteins in “Extended Data Fig. 2,4,6”. I don´t see these data anywhere in the submitted files.
Source data Fig. b (BGCs): It is nice, that the BGCs are displayed. However, these collections in the Excel sheet confuse me: Either, the arrow colors must be clearly explained, or better, cleaner SI Figures visualizing and aligning the BGCs should be provided.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript entitled "Evolutionary repurposing of a metabolic thiolase complex enables antibiotic biosynthesis" by Liao et al. presents an interesting and informative structural and functional investigation of SmaATase, a multimeric thiolase enzyme complex from S. macaca involved in the biosynthesis of the antimicrobial compound reutericyclin A. This secondary metabolic pathway is proposed to have evolved from the central metabolic pathway for mevalonate biosynthesis in archaea by functionally repurposing the tripartite enzyme complex that couples 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase (HMGS) and acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase (ACAT) reactivity. Biochemical characterization of SmaATase revealed the HMGS activity of the proposed archaeal ancestor was lost, and instead of Claisen condensation activity the ACAT homolog catalyzes a non-canonical Friedel-Crafts C-acetylation on a pyrrolidine-2,4-dione scaffold. This is similar to another bacterial tripartite enzyme complex, PpATase from P. protogens, that performs a Friedel-Crafts C-acylation of monoacetylphloroglucinol (MAPG) to diacetylphloroglucinol (DAPG, an antimicrobial compound) and phloroglucinol (PG). Notably, although the HMGS activity of the archaeal ancestor is not preserved in SmaATase or PpATase, the authors were only able to observe the C-acetylation activity in the presence of the complete tripartite complex, suggesting the evolutionary trajectory may have prioritized chemical specialization over quaternary structural modifications. This point is further illustrated by comparison of experimental structures, including new cryo-EM results of SmaATase, that show strong structural similarities in the overall subunit organization and Co-A binding site, and all complexes contain the canonical thiolase ⍺β⍺β⍺ fold. Multiple sequence alignment reveals SmaATase and PpATase retain some, but not all, sequence motifs characteristic of ACATs, and they lack a conserved sequence essential for HGMS activity. Biochemical activity assays of wild type and generated mutants shed light on the functional roles of various sequence motifs. Finally, they find that the acetylation modification to form RTC-A and DAPG is critical for antimicrobial potency against competitors, implicating the vital importance of these bacterial ATases. The results have broad importance across fields of biosynthesis and bioengineering, and I recommend for publication after addressing the following issues/comments that would improve this manuscript primarily in terms of clarity, discussion depth, and reproducibility.
Major Comments
1. Docking studies are performed, but interpretation and presentation of the results are lacking. No data/results are presented besides SI Fig. 23 which does not provide substantial information. Line 237 states “Docking results showed that conserved C87 and H349 may coordinate catalysis, while H143, Y300, and Q302 support substrate positioning”. How? C87 and H349 are not depicted in SI Fig. 23a, and H143, Y300, and Q302 are only depicted as “contact residues”. Are there truly no more hydrogen bonds to the ligand besides with Tyr300 (SI Fig. 23a)? Do the docking results show many or few binding conformations? This manuscript could be greatly benefit from an explanation of the reaction mechanism catalyzed by PpATase (steps detailed in the manuscript Ref. 25) and based on that the authors can discuss the likely residues of the SmaATase active site that are involved in the reaction. The differences between these two active sites, and their deviation from archaeal ACAT discussed from the mechanistic perspective would certainly enhance the manuscript’s argument of functional repurposing.
2. MD simulations are performed, but interpretation and presentation of the results are lacking. SI Fig 23b is not discussed anywhere. In particular, the per-residue RMSF appears to show that many active site residues have high fluctuations. Typically, when a binder is present we might expect active site rigidity, especially if the molecule is stably bound.
3. Simulations were performed with only MucB, not the full complex, which was shown to be required for activity. Did the authors perform any binding kinetics with only MucB, or have reason to believe MucB can effectively bind the substrate, and in the same way it would if the complex was formed? It is interesting that the MM/GBSA binding free energy calculations show favorable binding to MucB, but experimental results (line 166) “suggest that while MucA and MucC may not directly participate in catalysis, they are essential for proper folding and assembly of the tripartite complex, thereby enabling its enzymatic activity”. Some discussion about the implications of these two results should be included to strengthen the manuscript.
4. The energy minimized coordinates of the ligand used in docking should be provided for reproducibility, as well as at least one set of xyz coordinates from the docking/simulation results of the holo enzyme.
5. The assigned protonation states used for simulations should be stated in the SI for the method to be transparent and reproducible. Additionally, the protonation state of residues in the binding site are likely significant. Some justification of choice should be provided, or evaluation of various possible states to ensure results are robust, but since these results are not critical for the manuscripts main objectives additional calculations could be avoided.
Minor Comments
1. DUF35 is not defined.
2. Line 91: Why was the MucABC sequence from S. mutans was used for the query instead of S. macaca? Since the paper focuses on the S. macaca complex it would be more consistent to use those results and likely does not alter any discussion.
3. Lines 128-129: Results for acetyl-CoA as a donor are stated. The reader would benefit from the results of the other physiologically relevant donors also being quickly stated.
4. Lines 134-135: “Together, these results support acetyl-CoA as the physiological acetyl donor…”. This may be too strong of a statement. First, it appears there is some, albeit very little, product formation with donors acetoacetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA (Fig. 1b). Second, are the donors evaluated the only physiological possibilities? Third, a previous study found no product with PpATase and acetyl-CoA. Either more justification should be included in the text to convince the reader that acetyl-CoA is THE donor, or the statement can be modified. Additionally, some discussion on why product was found using PpATase with acetyl-CoA when a previous study found this did not work is warranted.
5. “r.m.s.d” should be RMSD throughout manuscript.
6. Line 179: The use of the word “mirrors” here could cause confusion as it implies chiral partners. “Resembles” would be a safer choice.
7. Line 192: Replace “substitutions” with “modifications” or similar, since the differences are more signification than single AA substitutions.
8. Line 218: “While no other function predictable…” This sentence was awkward to understand- could be written more clearly.
9. Line 239: E124 and S142 are not hydrophobic residues.
10. Line 240: Reference needed for W211 in Ph1C proposed to act as conformational lid.
11. Line 275: The reactions of SmaATase and PpATase are not “single-step” (particularly because they involve acylation and deacylation phases that are likely both multi-step reactions). Do the authors mean single reactions, as opposed to coupled reactions?
12. Line 435: What pH was assumed for protonation state assignment?
13. Line 435: Is “hydrogenated” an appropriate term here? Do the authors mean they modeled in unresolved H atoms to the structure?
14. Line 440: Can the authors provide more information beyond “Phad Calculation Co., Ltd”? I tried searching for this company and could not find any results.
15. Line 442: ff19SB needs reference and AMBER Tools needs reference.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewers' Comments to Author:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author)
Comments:
In their manuscript, Liao et al study bacterial tripartite complex systems analogous to the
thiolase/HMG-CoA synthase/DUF-35 protein used by archaea to catalyse the first steps of
isoprenoid synthesis. Through an impressive panel of methods ranging from enzymology,
structural biology, biochemistry, bioinformatics, phylogeny, and even genome mining, they
found that the thiolase subunit from the bacterial homologues from Streptomyces macacae
(SmaATase) and from Pseudomonas protegens (PpATase) catalyse a rare Friedel-Crafts
reaction involving acetyl-CoA as acetyl donor. The end products of these reactions
ultimately generate molecules with antibiotic activities. It is without any doubt a study of
high quality, bringing to light an enzymatic complex involved in secondary metabolism that
most probably originates from a central carbon metabolism involved in isoprenoid
biosynthesis. The reviewer congratulates the authors on this excellent study that reaches
the standard of Nature Communications, and would strongly support its publication upon
addressing these minor comments.
1- Abstract: “Cryo-electron microscopy of the S. macaca-derived thiolase complex”.
Shouldn´t it be S. macacae instead of S. macaca?
Response:
We have corrected the species name to S. macacae in the abstract.
2- Title of the result first subsection. “Characterization of Streptococcal ATases as non-
canonical Friedel-Crafts acylases”. For clarification, it would be helpful to state the meaning
of “ATases” here or before instead of using the abbreviation. Moreover, since the
physiological donor is acetyl-CoA, authors should consider using the term acetylases
instead of acylases.
Response:
Clarification of the ATase as acyltransferase was added in the title of first result subsection:
“Characterization of Streptococcal acyltransferases (ATases) as non-canonical
Friedel-Crafts acylases”.
We agree that “acetylase” is a more precise term when considering that acetyl-CoA is the
primary physiological donor. However, our enzyme assays demonstrate that SmaATase
exhibits activity with acyl donors of up to C8 chain length (as detailed in the attached file
for reviewers), indicating its catalytic scope extends beyond acetylation. Therefore, we
have chosen to use the broader and established term “acylase”, which encompasses
acetylase and is consistent with the nomenclature used for the related enzyme PpATase
(ChemBioChem 2019, 20, 88–95).
3- Legend of Supplementary Fig. 2c. “SDS-PAGE analysis of the heterologous expression
and purification results of SmaATase, SmuATase, and StrATase, respectively. SmaATase,
SmuATase, and StrATase represent MucABC enzyme complex from S. mutans, S.
macacae, S. troglodytae, respectively.”
Based on the text and results, it should be: “SDS-PAGE analysis of the heterologous
expression and purification results of SmaATase, SmuATase, and StrATase, respectively.
SmaATase, SmuATase, and StrATase represent MucABC enzyme complex from S.
macacae, S. mutans, S. troglodytae, respectively.”
Response:
The correction has been made as suggested.
4- 2nd paragraph results: “Additionally, MucABC-mediated reverse conversion of RTC-A
back to preRTC-A was observed, confirming the bidirectionality of the reaction
(Supplementary Fig. 6d).” Would it be possible to provide the Standard Gibbs free energy
for the reaction? That would provide some insights on its expected directionality.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this point regarding the reaction’s bidirectionality. Our
follow-up investigations indicate that determining a ΔG°' value is not feasible because the
reverse reaction is kinetically blocked by the enzyme’s substrate specificity.
In the forward direction, SmaATase accepts acetyl-CoA or phenyl acetate (PA) as acetyl
donors and transfers the acetyl group to preRTC-A. In contrast, the enzyme cannot
efficiently use CoA or phenol as acetyl acceptors in the reverse direction. Incubation of
SmaATase with RTC-A and either CoA or phenol did not yield more preRTC-A than the
control (see new Supplementary Fig. 7a).
The “reverse” activity we observed is in fact a transacetylation reaction. As demonstrated
in revised Supplementary Fig. 7b and 7c, when provided with a suitable structural analog
(preRTC-C2) as an acetyl acceptor, SmaATase catalyzes acetyl group transfer from RTC-
A to form preRTC-A and RTC-C2. This demonstrates that the enzyme can cleave the C–C
bond in RTC-A, thereby enabling it to function as an acetyl donor. A similar capability has
been reported for PpATase when using MAPG and DAPG as acetyl donors.
Accordingly, we have revised the statement to: “Additionally, MucABC-mediated
conversion of RTC-A to preRTC-A was observed, indicating that the C–C bond
formed by MucABC is cleavable by the enzyme, thereby enabling RTC-A to serve as
an acetyl donor in a transacetylation reaction (Supplementary Fig. 7).”
5- 3rd paragraph results: “Notably, earlier studies reported no detectable product formation
when PpATase was incubated with acetyl-CoA”. By curiosity, do the authors have an
explanation for why the activity was not observable before with acetyl-CoA?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for their curiosity regarding this discrepancy. We agree that
providing a possible explanation is important.
In the first study (Biosci. Biotech. Bioch. 2012, 76: 559), enzyme activity was monitored
spectrophotometrically at 370 nm—an indirect and relatively insensitive approach that may
not detect low turnover rates. In the later study (ChemCatChem 2019, 11: 1064), HPLC
detection was performed at 254 nm. Our data show that this wavelength is suboptimal for
specifically detecting MAPG and DAPG, whereas our UPLC-based assay at 280 nm
provides a substantially stronger and more selective signal (see the figure below).
Additionally, the HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex is known to be unstable during storage; for
example, the archaeal homolog retains only ~15% activity after two weeks at –80 °C
(PNAS 2018, 115: 3380). The use of suboptimally preserved enzyme or insufficiently
sensitive detection methods in previous studies could therefore have resulted in a false-
negative outcome.
To avoid over-interpreting these methodological differences and to keep the focus on our
findings, we have removed the comparative statement about earlier studies from the
revised manuscript (see below).
