The figure (now is Supplementary Fig. 21) has been corrected as suggested.
15- 7th paragraph results: “). Additionally, a hallmark of the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35
complex is the presence of a fused CoA-binding site at the HMGS–ACAT interface, which
facilitates shuttling of the pantetheinyl arm between active sites during catalysis (Fig. 2f).”
A supplementary figure comparing the CoA binding site between the archaeal
ACAT/HMGS/DUF-35 protein (PDB 6ESQ) and SmaATase would reinforce the observation
made on Fig. 2f. Are most of the residues conserved? Also, please correct the typo on Fig.
2f “fused Co-A binding” should be “fused CoA-binding”.
Response:
We agree with the reviewer that a detailed structural comparison of the CoA-binding sites
would strengthen the interpretation presented Fig. 2f.
The previous study on the archaeal complex (PNAS 2018, 115: 3380) revealed the novel
architectural principle of a fused CoA-binding site that couples the ACAT (thiolase)
and HMGS reactions (see below Fig. i). Although the study illustrated a few candidate
residues (C206, K332 in ACAT; R203, K243, K247 in HMGS) proximal to CoA in a figure
(see below Fig. ii) through comparison with the CoA-substrate binding sites of lone-standing
thiolase and HMGS, their specific functional roles were not experimentally validated and
were not discussed in detail in the publication.
Our residue-level comparison indicates that while some residues (e.g., K332, R203, K243)
are conserved in archaea, others (such as C206 and K247) are not (see below Fig. iii).
The corresponding positions in SmaATase also differ, suggesting that although the spatial
architecture of the binding pocket is conserved, the exact residue composition is not
identical between the two complexes.
To provide a clear and objective visualization of these similarities and differences, we have
added a new supplementary figure (Supplementary Fig. 23) showing a side-by-side
comparison of the CoA-binding interface in SmaATase and the archaeal homolog. This
figure highlights both the conserved structural arrangement and the variations in residue
identity.
Finally, as suggested, the typo in Fig. 2f has been corrected from “fused Co-A binding” to
“fused CoA-binding”.
16- 11th paragraph results: “Introducing an H294Y mutation in PfACAT nearly abolished
this activity (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 20), confirming the essential catalytic role of
the His residue within the HDxF motif.”. This is a very interesting point. Are the authors
expecting a role in antibiotic biosynthesis for this enzyme? It is unlikely that its physiological
function would be simply the formation of acetyl-CoA from acetoacetyl-CoA. The latter
might simply be a side reaction.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this intriguing question regarding the physiological
function of the PfACAT/HMGS-DUF35 complex.
We agree that its in vivo function is unlikely to be simply the thiolytic cleavage of
acetoacetyl-CoA. Instead, we propose that the thiolase activity observed in vitro may
represent a residual biochemical capability of the ACAT domain, rather than its primary
physiological role.
Although PfACAT/HMGS-DUF35 retains the ancestral HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 architectural
framework, key mutations in catalytic tetrad E-C-H-N have inactivated the HMGS domain.
This loss of HMGS activity disrupts the canonical function of the complex in the mevalonate
pathway. The reaction catalyzed by ACAT (2×Acetyl-CoA ⇌ Acetoacetyl-CoA + CoA) is
highly endergonic (ΔG°' = +26.1 kJ/mol) with a small equilibrium constant [Keq = (1.1 ±
0.2)×10-5] (PNAS 2018, 115: 3380), strongly favoring the thiolytic direction. Thus, in the
absence of a functional HMGS domain capable of consuming acetoacetyl-CoA, the
reaction defaults toward thiolysis—consistent with what we observed in vitro.
Genomic context also argues against a role in classical antibiotic biosynthesis. Unlike
PpATase or SmaATase, the PfACAT/HMGS–DUF35 locus lacks adjacent PKS, NRPS, or
hybrid biosynthetic genes typically associated with HMGS–ACAT–DUF35 complexes
engaged in secondary metabolism. This genomic isolation makes its direct participation in
canonical natural product biosynthesis unlikely. While the available data do not support
recruitment of PfACAT/HMGS–DUF35 into a known antibiotic biosynthetic pathway, we
cannot exclude the possibility that it participates in an uncharacterized specialized
metabolic process that operates independently of PKS/NRPS systems.
In conclusion, we propose that PfACAT/HMGS–DUF35 represents an evolutionary
intermediate: a complex that has diverged from its primary metabolic role but has not been
co-opted into a specialized biosynthetic pathway like its bacterial homologs. We have
revised the manuscript to incorporate this evolutionary interpretation.
17- Figure 5: Cys88 is acetylated, please label the residue accordingly (e.g., Acetyl-C88).
D137 cited in the text is not shown on the figure. Importantly, the difference in the active
site pose confuses the reader as it seems that the orientation between PpATase and
SmaATase is the same, but the position of the residues (particularly C88/H347 and
C87/H349) is different. Please take a new picture with the exact same orientation between
PpATase and SmaATase active sites. Highlight the key residues C88/H347 and C87/H349
with a bold label.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for these precise suggestions to improve the clarity of the figure. All
suggested changes have been implemented in the revised Figure 5.
18- Supplementary Fig. 23: Why is the hydrogen bond not shown for Q302? Is there a
possibility to switch the H143 rotamer to gain a hydrogen bond with the ligand without
generating steric clashes? Here, 4.1 A seems too distant for efficient
Response:
The discrepancy in hydrogen bond depiction between Fig. 5 and the original
Supplementary Fig. 23 was due to differences in the visualization algorithms used by the
two software packages.
To establish a more reliable substrate-binding model, we re-performed the molecular
docking and dynamics simulations using an improved system. Specifically, we employed
the complete MucA-B-C complex bound to the native substrate preRTC-A, rather than the
previously used standalone MucB subunit with a truncated analog. The updated results
demonstrate that H143 mediates hydrophobic contacts with the substrate rather than
forming a direct hydrogen bond (Fig. 5); the overall binding of preRTC-A is stabilized by
hydrogen bonds with Y300 and H349 (Fig. 5), supplemented by hydrophobic and van der
Waals interactions with other surrounding residues (revised Supplementary Fig. 27).
To present these findings clearly, hydrogen bonds are depicted in the 3D structural
overview (Fig. 5), and we now provide a dedicated 2D ligand–interaction diagram in
revised Supplementary Fig. 27 summarizing all hydrophobic and van der Waals contacts.
19- Supplementary Fig. 24: The final concentration of the used compounds must be stated
in the figure or legend.
Response:
The final concentration of the tested compounds (400 μg/mL) has been added to the
legend of revised Supplementary Fig. 30.
20- Last paragraph of the result section: “Although preRTC-A showed modest activity
against S. gordonii ATCC 10558 (MIC = 32 μg/mL), RTC-A demonstrated a 32-fold
enhancement in potency (MIC = 1 μg/mL; Fig. 6). A similar trend was observed for the
phenolic polyketide DAPG and its biosynthetic precursor PG. DAPG exhibited significantly
higher antimicrobial activity against most tested strains (except S. oralis DA1241 and S.
gordonii ATCC 10558) compared to PG, recapitulating the structure–activity relationship
observed for RTC-A and preRTC-A pair (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 24).”. The whole
sentence should be clarified. The results obtained are excellent, and authors should rather
use a general statement to describe the results, for instance: All strains showed inhibition
for DAPG compared to PG, except S. gordonii and S. oralis. The effect is even more
pronounced for preRTC-A versus RTC-A, where all tested strains showed inhibition for
RTA-A compared to preRTC-A.”
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. The text has been revised for clarity and
conciseness (see below).
21- 1st paragraph discussion: “In contrast, SmaATase is remarkable for its ability to
catalyze Friedel–Crafts acylation independently of CoA or ACP-activated acyl donors,
highlighting its potential as a versatile biocatalyst for synthetic applications.” The
acetylation is CoA-dependent. Please rephrase.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important clarification. We agree that, in vivo, acetyl-CoA is
the physiological acetyl donor for SmaATase and therefore the native acetylation reaction
is CoA-dependent.
Our intention in the original sentence was to emphasize a biochemical capability of
SmaATase revealed by our in vitro assays that SmaATase is not strictly restricted to acetyl-
CoA as an acetyl donor. As shown in Fig. 1b, the enzyme can utilize several alternative
donors, including N-acetylimidazole, isopropenyl acetate, ethyl thioacetate, and phenyl
acetate. This donor promiscuity distinguishes SmaATase from canonical acyltransferases
that rely exclusively on CoA or ACP-activated acyl donors.
To avoid ambiguity and better reflect this point, we have reivsed the sentence to: “In
contrast, SmaATase exhibits remarkable promiscuity toward acetyl donors,
catalyzing Friedel–Crafts acylation with not only the canonical donor acetyl-CoA but
also with unnatural donors such as phenyl acetate.”
22- 2nd paragraph discussion: “…enzyme complexes in secondary metabolism are more
commonly associated with scaffold formation (such as PKS37 and NRPS38) than with
structural modification”. What is the meaning of structural modification here? Please
reformulate.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity. In the original sentence, “structural
modification” referred to post-assembly tailoring reactions in secondary metabolism—such
as methylation, prenylation, hydroxylation, and glycosylation—that decorate or remodel the
core scaffold after its initial construction.
Our intention was to contrast the quaternary structure complexity of enzyme complexes
involved in scaffold assembly (e.g., PKSs and NRPSs, which are large, multi-domain
megasynthases) with the generally simpler architecture of enzymes responsible for
tailoring modifications, which are typically monomeric, dimeric, or form only small
oligomers. In this context, the discovery of SmaATase as a hetero-oligomeric complex
dedicated to an acetylation tailoring reaction is therefore noteworthy.
To remove ambiguity, we have reformulated the sentence in the manuscript to: “... enzyme
complexes in secondary metabolism are more commonly associated with the
primary assembly of carbon skeletons scaffold formation (such as PKS37 and
NRPS38) than with the post-assembly tailoring reactions (e.g., methylation,
prenylation, hydroxylation).”
23- Supplementary Fig. 25: It would help the reader to add the acetylated cysteine residue
position in the three studied systems (in the figure or in the legend).
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. The positions of the acetylated cysteine residues
in the three studied systems have been added to the figure (now is Supplementary Fig.
31).
24- Methods, protein expression and purification: “and imaged using the DelDoc Go
system (Bio-Rad).”. It should be GelDoc Go system.
Response:
Done.
25- Methods, Cryo-EM structural determination: Please provide the following information.
Protein concentration and buffer used for the grid.
How did authors build, refine, and validate the model?
“Ab-initio reconstruction of these particles produced an octameric structure at 2.16 Å
resolution.” Ab initio is not a refinement technique, so it does not make sense to associate
ab initio with resolution. Please reformulate.
Response:
As requested, the methods section has been updated to include the protein concentration
(3.8 mg/mL) and buffer composition (50 mM potassium phosphate, pH 7.5) used for grid
preparation.
We have expanded the description of the model building, refinement, and validation
procedures to provide a more comprehensive account of the workflow.
Besides, the sentence “Ab-initio reconstruction of these particles produced an octameric
structure at 2.16 Å resolution.” has been revised to: “Ab-initio reconstruction of these
particles produced an octameric structure, and the resolution of this structure
reaches 2.16 Å after non-uniform refinement.”
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Xiaoyu Tang and colleagues present a manuscript detailing the biochemical
characterization of a tripartite enzymatic complex catalyzing Friedel-Crafts-Acylation in the
biosynthesis of the antibiotic tetramate reutericyclin A. This enzymatic complex bears
similarities to a previously characterized system able to catalyze acetylation of
phloroglucinol. The protein complex was structurally characterized via Cryo-EM, revealing
a dodecameric structure, analogous to a previously characterized pathway in archaeal
mevalonate biosynthesis. Bioinformatic analyses showed that key catalytic residues of the
primary metabolism enzyme were lost, and new, potentially critical residues for a new
catalytic functon(acetylation) acquired. Based on these findings, the authors pose the
hypothesis that the enzymatic complex was repurposed during evolution to acquire a new
catalytic function. Finally, the authors show that acetylation is an essential feature for
antibiotic activity in both reutericyclins and phloroglucinols, highlighting the biological
importance of this modification.
The paper is very well and clearly written and contains a lot of data. The experiments were
carried out with a range of state-of the-art methodologies, and the results are nicely
presented in main and SI Figures. Overall, this study deserves publication in Nature
Communications. However, there are a couple of issues that should be improved or taken
care of before publication:
Major:
l.265: SmaATase is praised having potential as a “versatile biocatalyst for synthetic
applications.” Indeed, the possible use of different acetyl donors has been demonstrated,
but the substrate scope has not been investigated at all to my understanding, except for
the acetylation of the native substrate pre-RTC and its short chain analogue. Of course, a
comprehensive enzymatic study is beyond the scope of this paper, but it would be nice to
provide some initial characterization: e.g. on simplified pyrrolidones with a few different
substituents. Also, I wonder, if propionyl chains could be accepted?
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments regarding the biocatalytic
potential of SmaATase.
Our description of SmaATase as a “versatile biocatalyst” was motivated by two
observations: (1) its ability to catalyze Friedel–Crafts C-acylation, a reaction scarcely
observed in enzymology; and (2) its capacity to utilize simple and inexpensive acetyl
donors, including phenyl acetate, in contrast to most acyltransferases that rely strictly on
CoA-activated donors.
Additionally, compared with PpATase—the first reported Friedel-Crafts acylase, which
display strict to resorcinol-containing substrates—SmaATase accepts preRTC-A, a
chemically distinct pyrrolidine-2,4-dione scaffold. This distinction suggests that the two
enzymes may offer complementary opportunities for biocatalysis.
We fully agree with the reviewer that a systematically evaluation of substrate scope would
be essential for defining the enzyme’s synthetic utility. In our preliminary assays,
SmaATase showed notable flexibility: (a) it accepts preRTC-A analogs with varying N-acyl
chain lengths (C2–C8) or different amino-acid-derived side chains as acceptors; (b) it also
utilizes phenyl esters with acyl chains up to C8 as donors. These data have been provided
to the reviewers in the attached file.
However, conducting a comprehensive substrate-scope study is beyond the scope of the
current work, which focuses primarily on the evolutionary repurposing of the thiolase
complex. To avoid overstating the biocatalytic implications, we have removed the phrase
“versatile biocatalyst for synthetic applications” from the revised manuscript, while
maintaining a factual description of the enzyme’s observed donor flexibility.
Figure 3b: The loss of key catalytic residues of primary metabolic enzymes has been
shown, but I am missing a Figure, where the acquisition of key residues for the new
catalytic function(see Figure 5, Fig. S23) is analyzed. It would be good to provide a similar
Figure and underlying alignments for these residues in primary vs. secondary metabolism.
Do all 31 enzymes contain the same sequence motifs in this region or are there variations?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this excellent suggestion. We agree that examining the
acquisition of key residues—in addition to the loss of ancestral primary-metabolism
residues—provides a more complete understanding of the functional repurposing process.
In response, we conducted a new comparative sequence analysis focusing on the active-
site residues that may contribute to the evolved acylation activity and substrate specificity.
The analysis highlights both the conserved catalytic machinery and the divergent
substrate-binding features that underlie functional specialization (Supplementary Figure
28, and we also included this figure on below).
Catalytically essential residues in PpATase map directly onto those in SmaATase: the
nucleophile C88 (PhlC) corresponds to C87 (MucB); the general base E116 corresponds
to D115; and the proton-relay network D137-T132-H144 corresponds to D136-T131-H143.
This conservation supports a shared catalytic mechanism between the two bacterial
enzymes that differs from the archaeal ACAT/HMGS complex.
By contrast, the substrate-binding pocket shows clear reconfiguration. Key PhlC substrate-
binding residues (H56, Y124, W211, Y298, H347) are either conserved (Y300, H349) or
replaced (A55, F123, A210) in MucB, whereas residues crucial for preRTC-A binding in
MucB (N86, M127, I144, Y300, H349) are conserved (N87, Y298, H347) or substituted
(I128, T145) in PhlC. These differences illustrate how the binding pocket was remodeled,
enabling SmaATase and PpATase to recognize distinct chemical scaffolds. We have
begun exploring several site-directed mutants in this region; however, these did not alter
substrate preference, suggesting that the molecular determinants of specificity are more
complex than initially anticipated and warrant further investigation.
Figure 4b,c and corresponding main text l.218-230: This part is not entirely clear to me:
The first sentence “While no other function predictable Friedel–Crafts acylases were
identified” makes no sense to me. Also, to me it is not clear, why the enzyme from P.
fluorescens was selected for further analysis. The rationale behind this experiment should
be better explained, as well the meaning of the obtained results.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the lack of clarity in this section and for prompting
us to improve the explanation.
The original sentence “While no other function predictable Friedel–Crafts acylases were
identified” has been removed from the manuscript. Our intention was simply to convey that
our genome-mining survey did not reveal any additional, easily predictable Friedel–Crafts
acylases beyond the known PpATase- and SmaATase-type enzymes.
We selected the PfACAT/HMGS–DUF35 complex from the 1,032 identified BGCs for
further analysis because it represents a major but previously uncharacterized class. It is a
minimal cluster that lacks canonical secondary metabolic partners (PKS/NRPS) but
features a fused HMGS-DUF35 protein (Fig. 4b). More importantly, sequence alignment
revealed a strikingly asymmetric conservation of catalytic features: (a) the HMGS domain
lacks the essential E–C–H–N catalytic tetrad, indicating that this module is inactive, while
(b) the ACAT domain retains the catalytic cysteine as well as the conserved HDxF and GHx
motifs (Fig. 3b).
Our biochemical data confirmed this prediction. The PfACAT/HMGS–DUF35 complex does
not catalyze the HMGS reaction, but retains thiolase activity, converting acetoacetyl-CoA
to acetyl-CoA—an activity not observed in SmaATase or PpATase (Fig. 4c).
Together, these findings support the interpretation that the PfACAT/HMGS–DUF35
complex represents a plausible evolutionary intermediate—one that has diverged from its
role in primary metabolism but has not yet been recruited into a canonical secondary
metabolic pathway.
The narrative in this section has been revised accordingly in the manuscript (Please see
lines 218 to 237).

Response:
Done.

We have now revised Fig. 3a to clearly label the corresponding branch as “MucC/PhlB and
homologs”, ensuring that the figure is fully consistent with the description in the main text.

these data anywhere in the submitted files.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author)
The manuscript entitled "Evolutionary repurposing of a metabolic thiolase complex enables
antibiotic biosynthesis" by Liao et al. presents an interesting and informative structural and
functional investigation of SmaATase, a multimeric thiolase enzyme complex from S.
macaca involved in the biosynthesis of the antimicrobial compound reutericyclin A. This
secondary metabolic pathway is proposed to have evolved from the central metabolic
pathway for mevalonate biosynthesis in archaea by functionally repurposing the tripartite
enzyme complex that couples 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase (HMGS) and
acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase (ACAT) reactivity. Biochemical characterization of SmaATase
revealed the HMGS activity of the proposed archaeal ancestor was lost, and instead of
Claisen condensation activity the ACAT homolog catalyzes a non-canonical Friedel-Crafts
C-acetylation on a pyrrolidine-2,4-dione scaffold. This is similar to another bacterial
tripartite enzyme complex, PpATase from P. protogens, that performs a Friedel-Crafts C-
acylation of monoacetylphloroglucinol (MAPG) to diacetylphloroglucinol (DAPG, an
antimicrobial compound) and phloroglucinol (PG). Notably, although the HMGS activity of
the archaeal ancestor is not preserved in SmaATase or PpATase, the authors were only
able to observe the C-acetylation activity in the presence of the complete tripartite complex,
suggesting the evolutionary trajectory may have prioritized chemical specialization over
quaternary structural modifications. This point is further illustrated by comparison of
experimental structures, including new cryo-EM results of SmaATase, that show strong
structural similarities in the overall subunit organization and Co-A binding site, and all
complexes contain the canonical thiolase ⍺β⍺β⍺ fold. Multiple sequence alignment reveals
SmaATase and PpATase retain some, but not all, sequence motifs characteristic of ACATs,
and they lack a conserved sequence essential for HGMS activity. Biochemical activity
assays of wild type and generated mutants shed light on the functional roles of various
sequence motifs. Finally, they find that the acetylation modification to form RTC-A and
DAPG is critical for antimicrobial potency against competitors, implicating the vital
importance of these bacterial ATases. The results have broad importance across fields of
biosynthesis and bioengineering, and I recommend for publication after addressing the
following issues/comments that would improve this manuscript primarily in terms of clarity,
discussion depth, and reproducibility.
Major Comments
1. Docking studies are performed, but interpretation and presentation of the results are
lacking. No data/results are presented besides SI Fig. 23 which does not provide
substantial information. Line 237 states “Docking results showed that conserved C87 and
H349 may coordinate catalysis, while H143, Y300, and Q302 support substrate
positioning”. How? C87 and H349 are not depicted in SI Fig. 23a, and H143, Y300, and
Q302 are only depicted as “contact residues”. Are there truly no more hydrogen bonds to
the ligand besides with Tyr300 (SI Fig. 23a)? Do the docking results show many or few
binding conformations? This manuscript could be greatly benefit from an explanation of the
reaction mechanism catalyzed by PpATase (steps detailed in the manuscript Ref. 25) and
based on that the authors can discuss the likely residues of the SmaATase active site that
are involved in the reaction. The differences between these two active sites, and their
deviation from archaeal ACAT discussed from the mechanistic perspective would certainly
enhance the manuscript’s argument of functional repurposing.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thorough and constructive feedback. It has
prompted a substantial revision of our computational analyses.
We acknowledge the limitations of our initial docking model and have therefore re-
performed all docking and molecular dynamics simulations with major methodological
improvements:
(1) Full quaternary context: The system was reconstructed to include the MucB subunit
along with its neighboring MucA and MucC subunits, providing a more realistic active-site
environment (details were given in question 3).
(2) Incorporation of acetylated Cys87: Cys87 was modeled in its acetylated state as a
non-standard residue, consistent with the electron density and confirmed by LC–MS/MS
(new Supplementary Fig. 29). This correction was essential for accurate mechanistic
interpretation.
(3) Full-length substrate modeling: preRTC-A was modeled in its full native form rather
other a truncated analogue.
(4) Improved docking methodology: Docking was re-performed using DiffDock, and the
most representative poses were selected for analysis.
(5) Replicated dynamics simulations: Subsequent analyses were based on three
independent and replicated MD simulations to ensure statistical reliability.
The results of this refined workflow are now presented as follows: (1) Fig. 5 shows key
polar interactions identified by PyMOL analysis of the optimal docking pose; (2)
Supplementary Fig. 27 provides a comprehensive 2D interaction map (hydrophobic
contacts and van der Waals interactions) generated with ProLIF.
Importantly, following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have added a mechanistic comparison
between SmaATase and PpATase in the revised manuscript (lines 242–256). We
summarize the established catalytic steps of PpATase, map their equivalents in SmaATase,
and discuss how divergence from the archaeal ACAT active site supports functional
repurposing. This substantially strengthens the mechanistic argument of our study.
2. MD simulations are performed, but interpretation and presentation of the results are
lacking. SI Fig 23b is not discussed anywhere. In particular, the per-residue RMSF appears
to show that many active site residues have high fluctuations. Typically, when a binder is
present we might expect active site rigidity, especially if the molecule is stably bound.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. To improve transparency and
interpretation of the MD results, we have added the following explanatory sentence to the
Fig. 5 legend regarding the updated Supplementary Fig. 27 (formerly Fig. S23):
“The reliability of the simulated substrate-binding mode is supported by the
identification of specific protein-ligand interactions, alongside with the convergence
of the protein-ligand RMSD, the low residual flexibility (RMSF) in the binding pocket,
and the stable compactness (Rg) and solvent accessibility (SASA) (Supplementary
Fig. 27).”
Regarding the reviewer’s concern about the per-residue RMSF values: in the updated
simulations, we indeed observe measurable flexibility in several active-site residues. This
may reflect the intrinsic property of the binding pocket in MucB, which is situated at the
interface with MucA and MucC subunits (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 18b). Our in
vitro results also demonstrate that SmaATase accepts a broad spectrum of preRTC-A
analogs featuring varying acyl chain lengths and distinct amino acid side chains (These
experimental data have been provided to the reviewers in the attached file.). This evidence
also supports the conformational flexibility of the substrate-binding pocket.
3. Simulations were performed with only MucB, not the full complex, which was shown to
be required for activity. Did the authors perform any binding kinetics with only MucB, or
have reason to believe MucB can effectively bind the substrate, and in the same way it
would if the complex was formed? It is interesting that the MM/GBSA binding free energy
calculations show favorable binding to MucB, but experimental results (line 166) “suggest
that while MucA and MucC may not directly participate in catalysis, they are essential for
proper folding and assembly of the tripartite complex, thereby enabling its enzymatic
activity”. Some discussion about the implications of these two results should be included
to strengthen the manuscript.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Our initial simulations
focused on MucB extracted from the full complex under the assumption that it retained the
functional conformation of the catalytic pocket. We agree that this required refinement.
To directly address the reviewer’s question, we examined whether isolated MucB is
capable of binding the substrate. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) measurements
showed that MucB alone binds preRTC-A with a K of 6.04 × 10⁻⁶ M, which is comparable
D
to the affinity of the full SmaATase complex (2.52 × 10⁻⁶ M, Supplementary Fig. 18a).
However, isolated MucB is catalytically inactive, despite its ability to bind the substrate.
This apparent discrepancy can be explained by the structural organization of the active
site: as shown in Supplementary Fig. 18b, the catalytic pocket resides at the interface of
MucA, MucB, and MucC. Thus, MucB alone can bind the ligand, but cannot achieve the
catalytic geometry without the contributions of MucA and MucC, which help shape the
active-site architecture. In light of this, we have re-performed all molecular docking and MD
simulations using a model that includes MucB together with its adjacent MucA and MucC
subunits, providing a more realistic representation of the enzymatically competent state.
These revised results are now included in Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 27.
To reconcile the biochemical and computational findings, we propose that SmaATase
exhibits assembly-induced activation, a phenomenon well documented in other multimeric
systems. For example:
• In the archaeal HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex, isolated subunits are insoluble or inactive.
• In the proteasome, β-subunits are minimally active alone but become fully active only
upon correct assembly.
We have incorporated a description of the SPR results and the mechanistic implication into
the revised manuscript (lines 167–173), highlighting that while substrate binding can occur
in MucB alone, proper assembly of the tripartite complex is required to establish the
catalytically competent active-site configuration.
4. The energy minimized coordinates of the ligand used in docking should be provided for
reproducibility, as well as at least one set of xyz coordinates from the docking/simulation
results of the holo enzyme.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion regarding reproducibility. As requested,
the energy-minimized coordinates of the ligand (optimized at the B3LYP/def2-TZVP level
using ORCA) and representative XYZ coordinates from the DiffDock simulation of the holo-
enzyme have been provided in the figshare repository associated with this manuscript.
5. The assigned protonation states used for simulations should be stated in the SI for the
method to be transparent and reproducible. Additionally, the protonation state of residues
in the binding site are likely significant. Some justification of choice should be provided, or
evaluation of various possible states to ensure results are robust, but since these results
are not critical for the manuscripts main objectives additional calculations could be avoided.
Response:
In the revised Methods section, we have added a detailed description of the protonation-
state assignment. Protonation states for all ionizable residues were determined using
PropKa at neutral pH. Specifically, His305 and Asp35 in MucA, Glu57, Asp134, and Glu296
in MucB, and Glu70 in MucC were predicted to be protonated, while all other residues were
kept in their standard protonation states.
Minor Comments
1. DUF35 is not defined.

We have revised the main text to include a definition upon first use as: “DUF35 (Pfam
family PF01796, Domain of Unknown Function)”.
2. Line 91: Why was the MucABC sequence from S. mutans was used for the query instead
of S. macaca? Since the paper focuses on the S. macaca complex it would be more
consistent to use those results and likely does not alter any discussion.
Response:
We used the S. mutans MucABC sequence as the initial BLASTP query because this study
builds directly on our previous work on the S. mutans muc BGC (ACS Infect. Dis. 2020,
6:563; Microbiome 2023, 11:97), making it the natural starting point for our analysis. For
biochemical and structural characterization, however, we prioritized the S. macacae
homolog due to its superior protein purity and yield. Importantly, the two homologs share
extremely high sequence identity (89-99% for MucA/MucB and 100% for MucC), so the
choice of query sequence does not alter the BLASTP mining results or affect any
conclusions in the manuscript.
3. Lines 128-129: Results for acetyl-CoA as a donor are stated. The reader would benefit
from the results of the other physiologically relevant donors also being quickly stated.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. In response, we have revised the main text as
following:
4. Lines 134-135: “Together, these results support acetyl-CoA as the physiological acetyl
donor…”. This may be too strong of a statement. First, it appears there is some, albeit very
little, product formation with donors acetoacetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA (Fig. 1b). Second,
are the donors evaluated the only physiological possibilities? Third, a previous study found
no product with PpATase and acetyl-CoA. Either more justification should be included in
the text to convince the reader that acetyl-CoA is THE donor, or the statement can be
modified. Additionally, some discussion on why product was found using PpATase with
acetyl-CoA when a previous study found this did not work is warranted.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We agree that our original statement
that acetyl-CoA is “the physiological acetyl donor” was too strong and have revised the text
accordingly.
Our data indicates that acetyl-CoA is the most likely physiological donor, as it produces
clear and reproducible product formation in SmaATase-catalyzed reactions. In contrast,
other potential donors—acetoacetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA—generate only trace signals
(Fig. 1b). These minimal peaks may reflect very weak enzymatic activity toward these
donors or low-level non-enzymatic breakdown of acetoacetyl-CoA/malonyl-CoA into
acetyl-CoA. Given the extremely small magnitude of these signals and the robust activity
observed with acetyl-CoA, we consider the physiological relevance of the alternative
donors to be negligible. Accordingly, we have modified the relevant sentence to the more
cautious: “Together, these results support acetyl-CoA as the potential physiological
acetyl donor for both SmaATase and PpATase.”
Regarding the discrepancy with earlier studies reporting no detectable PpATase activity
with acetyl-CoA, the cited work provides insufficient methodological detail to identify the
precise cause. However, methodological differences offer a plausible explanation. In the
first study (Biosci. Biotech. Bioch. 2012, 76: 559), enzyme activity was monitored
spectrophotometrically at 370 nm—an indirect and relatively insensitive approach that may
not detect low turnover rates. In the later study (ChemCatChem 2019, 11: 1064), HPLC
detection was performed at 254 nm. Our data show that this wavelength is suboptimal for
specifically detecting MAPG and DAPG, whereas our UPLC-based assay at 280 nm
provides a substantially stronger and more selective signal (see the figure below).

Additionally, the HMGS/ACAT/DUF35 complex is known to be unstable during storage; for
example, the archaeal homolog retains only ~15 activity after two weeks at –80 °C
(PNAS 2018, 115: 3380). The use of suboptimally preserved enzyme or insufficiently
sensitive detection methods in previous studies could therefore have resulted in a false-
negative outcome.
To avoid over-interpreting these methodological differences and to keep the focus on our
findings, we have removed the comparative statement about earlier studies from the
revised manuscript (see below).

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have addressed most of the comments by me and also the other reviewers
(as far as I can judge) comprehensively and convincingly. There is only one remark to one
of my initial minor comments that has not been addressed, probably due to a
misunderstanding in nomenclature.
The comment "Fig. 3a: Why are MucC/PhlB homologues not included in the phylogenetic
tree?" was related to the lack of exactly these enzymes (DUF35 homologues) in the
phylogenetic tree. In the revised version, these are still missing in the tree, which has not
changed, as far as I can see. My question was pointing to if there is a particular reason for
excluding these from the phylogenetic analysis or if it would make sense to include them.
Response:
We sincerely apologize for the oversight of having confused MucC/PhlB with MucB/PhlC
in our previous response. The phylogenetic analysis in Fig. 3a was intended to reconstruct
the evolutionary relationships within the thiolase superfamily. MucA/PhlA belong to the
HMGS (hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA synthase) clade, and MucB/PhlC are members of the
ACAT (acetyl-CoA C-acetyltransferase) clade, both of which are established members of
the thiolase superfamily. In contrast, MucC/PhlB are classified under the DUF35 family
(domain of unknown function), which falls outside the thiolase superfamily. Therefore,
MucC/PhlB were not included in this analysis.
